analysis.one_liner: Lets people in counties with no ACA plans buy the same coverage Members of Congress get.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee, dying without a hearing or vote in the 115th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2017, a small number of counties had no health plans for sale on the Affordable Care Act exchanges at all, leaving residents with no way to use their federal coverage subsidies. This bill would have let people in those bare counties enroll instead through the small-group exchange in Washington, DC — the same market Members of Congress and their staff use — while keeping any premium tax credits or cost-sharing help they qualified for. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and received no further action before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of counties or rating areas where the Secretary of Health and Human Services certified that no exchange plan was offered — people who were eligible for ACA subsidies but had nothing to spend them on. They would gain a route into DC's small-group market, including the plan options available to Members of Congress and congressional staff [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of counties with no ACA plans

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires HHS, within three months of enactment, to set up a way for anyone living where no qualified health plan is offered on their state's exchange to enroll in small-group coverage through the DC exchange [S3].
It preserves their premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, so the money they were already eligible for follows them to the new coverage [S3].
The bill's stated purpose is to give these residents access similar to what Members of Congress and congressional staff have [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would keep paying the premium tax credits and cost-sharing help these individuals were already entitled to, and DC's small-group insurers would gain a small number of new enrollees in a guaranteed-issue group market, where costs are shared across all small-group customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal subsidy budgets and small-group insurance pools

drawbacks.text: The fix is narrow: it only helps people in counties with literally zero exchange plans, and does nothing about counties with one expensive insurer — the far more common affordability problem [S2].

Adding a small group of guaranteed-issue enrollees to DC's small-group market spreads their costs across that market's existing customers and premiums, and the bill sets no payment mechanism to offset that [S3].
It does not address whether the underlying plans are affordable — a bare-county resident moved into DC coverage could still face high premiums once subsidies were applied [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a targeted patch for a real but small failure: counties where the ACA marketplace had no product at all. The cost is modest and mostly a bookkeeping shift of subsidies people were already owed, with some premium pressure on DC's small-group pool. It was a genuine, if partial, fix — and its narrowness means it would have left most affordability problems untouched even had it passed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in May 2017, and the committee never took it up before the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Senator McCaskill introduced the bill on May 22, 2017, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
Three senators cosponsored the bill — two Democrats and one independent [S4].
The Finance Committee held no hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor during the 115th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the outcome; the residents of bare counties who could not use their subsidies remain where they were, and the status quo — which asked nothing of the committee or the insurance market — was preserved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no one acted on the bill

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought to give residents of counties without any exchange plans access to the same small-group coverage Members of Congress use.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Sen. Orrin Hatch)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all three cosponsors were Democrats or an independent, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have routed a small pool of new customers into DC's small-group plans, which already cover Members of Congress and staff. Because those residents would buy the same regulated plans the public uses, the industry's gain tracks with what people in bare counties needed.
